verdict.label: Proceed with Caution
verdict.summary: Adding one full-time kitchen/prep hire (~$4,625/mo loaded) plus roughly $1,350/mo more advertising (~$2,000/mo total ad spend) costs about $5,975/mo — but because your ovens already run at 100% on Fri-Sat peaks, this only pays off if the added labor and ads are pointed at off-peak catering (your +$15K/mo, 66.6%-margin lane) and weekday demand, not weekend dine-in; done that way you break even around month 3-4 and cash never approaches your $60K reserve floor (starting cash is $143,733).
verdict.reserve_warning: No reserve breach. Your lowest projected cash point in the 6-month horizon stays around $138K-$140K, far above your $60K target reserve. The risk here is wasted spend and margin drag if ads drive weekend dine-in demand your ovens physically cannot serve — not a cash/solvency risk.
verdict.confidence_reason: Based on historical financial trends and baseline data.

steps.title: Point the new hire and ads at catering + weekday, NOT weekend dine-in
steps.what: Structure this entire plan around your off-peak catering lane and weekday lunch/dinner, because your Fri-Sat ovens are already maxed at 100%.
steps.how: Task the new prep hire with morning catering-tray production and weekday lunch prep (before the 11:30 open) so catering output can scale toward the +$15K/mo headroom without touching Fri-Sat oven time. Set ad campaigns to run Tuesday-Friday and geo-fence Google 'catering near me' / 'corporate lunch catering Park Slope' search terms plus a Meta catering lead form — do NOT boost weekend dine-in posts.
steps.why: Your ovens run at 100% on peak — every extra weekend dine-in customer an ad attracts either walks away or waits longer, hurting reviews. The only place $5,975/mo of new cost earns a return is the ~$9,990/mo gross contribution available in unfilled catering capacity.
steps.decision_gate: If after 60 days catering inquiries are not translating to at least ~$4K/mo in booked trays, pause the extra ad spend before scaling it further.

steps.title: Right-size and cost the hire against real Brooklyn wages
steps.what: Hire one full-time prep/kitchen person and budget the fully-loaded cost, not just the sticker wage.
steps.how: Brooklyn line cook wages average about $20.52/hr and prep cooks about $19.32/hr; add roughly 30% for payroll taxes, workers' comp, and any benefits to reach a true ~$26.67/hr, or ~$4,625/mo full-time. Post on Indeed and Poached (the NYC restaurant hiring standard), and require ServSafe or offer to certify — it's often needed for catering food-safety compliance. Consider starting at 30 hrs/week to test the catering ramp before committing to 40.
steps.why: The fully-loaded number ($4,625/mo) — not the $20.52/hr headline — is what your break-even math depends on. Underestimating loading by even 20% would push your break-even a full month later.
steps.decision_gate: If catering demand is still building, start the hire part-time (30 hrs) — this drops the labor cost to ~$3,470/mo and pulls break-even earlier.

steps.title: Launch a tightly-tracked, catering-first ad program
steps.what: Split the added ~$1,350/mo between high-intent Google Search and a Meta catering lead-gen campaign, and track every dollar.
steps.how: Restaurant Google Search CPCs are cheap ($1.50-$2.05) and restaurant Google Ads average ~4.2x ROAS, so put ~$800/mo there on catering + 'pizza delivery Park Slope' weekday terms. Put ~$550/mo into a Meta catering lead form using UGC-style video of tray builds (food UGC earns a ~25% hook rate). Tag every catering lead source in Toast so you can measure cost-per-booked-order, not just clicks.
steps.why: General restaurant Meta ROAS is only ~2.2x, but catering-specific campaigns show far higher documented returns because a single corporate account is worth many transactions. At a conservative blended ~3x, $1,350 in new spend should return ~$4,050/mo in revenue and climb as catering accounts repeat.
steps.customer_experience_element: Catering revenue is won on the FIRST order and kept on repeats. On every first corporate order: include a handwritten thank-you from Tony, one free tray-upgrade or dessert box (a gift, not a discount), and a printed 'standing weekly order' card. Have Tony personally call the office manager 48 hours after their first event. Capture every catering contact into a simple list and send a Monday 'this week's lunch trays' text — office lunch decisions are made Monday morning.

steps.title: Protect the reserve and stage the spend
steps.what: Roll costs on in phases rather than all at once so you never commit ahead of demand.
steps.how: Month 1: start ads only ($1,350) and hire part-time. Month 2-3: move the hire to full-time once catering bookings cover at least their wage. Fund entirely from cash flow (+$11,650/mo) — no debt, consistent with your 'reinvest cash flow, zero high-interest debt' preference. Keep a hard line: never let cash drop below your $60K target.
steps.why: Staging means your worst realistic case (ads underperform at ~2x, catering ramps slowly) still leaves cash near $138K in month 2 — $78K above your floor. You are risking margin, not survival.
steps.decision_gate: If cash ever trends toward $75K (unlikely here), freeze ad spend and revert the hire to part-time immediately.

steps.title: Measure against a break-even dashboard monthly
steps.what: Track one number each month: incremental revenue from catering + weekday vs. the $5,975 combined cost.
steps.how: In Toast + QuickBooks, build a simple monthly line for 'new catering/weekday revenue' and compare to $8,970 (the revenue needed to cover $5,975 at 66.6% GM). Review on the 1st of each month.
steps.why: You need ~$8,970/mo in incremental revenue to break even. If you're not on a path to that by month 3, the plan needs rework — this dashboard tells you a month before cash would ever show strain.

things_to_keep_in_mind: 'Inventory workforce' isn't a standard pizzeria role — if you actually meant a purchasing/inventory-control person (to fight the 14% mozzarella/dairy inflation you flagged), that's a cost-reduction play with completely different math than a catering-prep hire. Tell me which and I'll rerun the right model.

New catering-prep labor also creates NYC food-handling obligations — the person handling off-premise trays should hold a NYC Food Protection Certificate, and corporate clients frequently require you to carry (and show a COI for) general liability, often $1M/$2M, before they'll sign.

Catering demand is intensely day-of-week and calendar-driven: office-lunch orders are decided Monday mornings, and December/June corporate event surges can collide with the very Fri-Sat oven crunch you're trying to avoid — batch and schedule catering bakes into your slow mid-week oven windows.

Restaurant ad ROAS benchmarks are compressing across the board in 2026, and a single Google 'near me' or Meta campaign under ~$450-$900/mo won't gather enough data to optimize — spread too thin and you learn nothing, so keep each channel funded above that learning threshold.

Your connected accounting currently shows an odd partial month (revenue_mtd $2,933, 100% gross margin) — that's early-month/demo noise, not reality. I modeled off your steady-state profile numbers; just be aware the live dashboard figure will look distorted until the month fills in.
data.peer_context: Based on national and category data for independent pizzerias and restaurant caterers (specific Park Slope-level performance data for this exact question was not available): restaurants are among the cheapest categories to advertise in, with Google CPCs of roughly $1.50-$2.05 versus a $5+ cross-industry average, and restaurant Google Ads average about 4.2x ROAS. Operators who succeed with a catering push consistently do two things right — they aim paid spend at high-intent 'catering near me' search rather than broad brand awareness, and they win on repeat corporate accounts (catering campaigns show documented ROAS well above the ~2.2x general restaurant Meta average). The ones who struggle spend into peak-demand periods their kitchen can't fulfill and treat catering as one-off transactions instead of recurring standing orders — exactly the trap your 100%-oven-utilization constraint makes it critical to avoid.
